You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Pearl

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching the pearl primarily symbolizes the kingdom of heaven (and by extension salvation, Christ, or the gospel) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing value — something worth surrendering everything else to obtain. This derives chiefly from Jesus' Parable of the Pearl of Great Price.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Matthew 13:45-46 (Parable of the Pearl of Great Price: the merchant sells all he has to buy the one pearl of great value)",
    "Matthew 7:6 ('do not cast your pearls before swine' — pearls as sacred truth or the precious things of God)",
    "Revelation 21:21 (the twelve gates of the New Jerusalem are each a single pearl, associating pearls with heavenly glory and entrance into God's presence)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The reversed reading of Matthew 13:45-46: Christ is the merchant and the pearl is the Church or the redeemed believer, purchased by Christ at the cost of everything (his life). Widely taught in evangelical and dispensational circles (e.g., popularized in older dispensational commentary traditions).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46",
        "1 Corinthians 6:20 / 1 Peter 1:18-19 (bought with a price, cited in support of Christ as the purchaser)",
        "Ephesians 5:25 (Christ gave himself for the church)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pearls as sacred truth, doctrine, or the gospel message that must not be profaned or offered to the contemptuous — from 'pearls before swine.' Often treated as a distinct application rather than a competing definition.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 7:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pearls as worldly luxury, wealth, and ostentation — a negative or cautionary symbol, especially in association with Babylon the harlot and warnings about adornment.",
      "basis": [
        "1 Timothy 2:9",
        "Revelation 17:4",
        "Revelation 18:12-16"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Patristic/allegorical readings identifying the one pearl specifically with Christ himself (sometimes linked to legends of the pearl's virgin birth from the oyster, used as an image of the Incarnation, e.g., in Ephrem the Syrian and other early writers).",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 13:45-46 as allegorized by church fathers (Origen, Ephrem the Syrian, Clement of Alexandria)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The pearl as the human soul or divine spark, as in the Gnostic 'Hymn of the Pearl' (Acts of Thomas); influential in history-of-religions scholarship but not part of orthodox Christian consensus.",
      "basis": [
        "Hymn of the Pearl in the Acts of Thomas (extra-biblical)"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a recognizable mainstream consensus that the pearl's central symbolic function is 'that which is of supreme value' — most commonly the kingdom of heaven/salvation per Matthew 13:45-46. However, the direction of the parable's allegory is genuinely disputed: the historically dominant reading makes the seeker the disciple and the pearl the kingdom, while a substantial popular tradition reverses it (Christ as merchant, believer/church as pearl). The negative usage (pearls as luxury in Revelation and 1 Timothy) is contextual rather than a competing core symbol. Prominence labels reflect published commentary, sermon literature, and Bible dictionaries; no single authoritative body fixes the meaning."
}

    },

        "Revelation 18:12,16"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"

  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a strong dominant association between pearls and exceptional spiritual preciousness, especially the supreme value of the kingdom in Matthew 13:45–46. However, there is no fully settled one-to-one symbolic referent across Scripture: context can make the pearl represent the kingdom, Christ, sacred truth, redeemed glory, or material luxury. Even within the pearl-of-great-price parable, interpreters differ over whether the pearl specifically represents the kingdom or Christ, and whether the merchant represents the seeker or Christ."
}

  "notes": "The parable supplies the dominant Christian symbolic association; secondary uses (Matt 7:6; Rev 21) are also standard. Allegorical details of the parable (who is the merchant, what exactly is the pearl) vary by tradition but do not displace the core sense of supreme value."
}

BOOK ENTRY
The one complete light — under the KJV's “rubies” (peninim, Strong's pearl), wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls; and the night sky's one pearl is the full moon (keseh, “fulness,” the letters under “throne” and “time appointed”), governor of the appointed times, the one-pearl gates of the city — the merchant's entry at the King's gate.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the kingdom of heaven, worth surrendering everything to gain — or the church, purchased by Christ.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Proverbs 3:15 — She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.
Proverbs 31:10 — Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
Psalms 81:3 — Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day.
Proverbs 7:20 — He hath taken a bag of money with him, and will come home at the day appointed.
Job 26:9 — He holdeth back the face of his throne, and spreadeth his cloud upon it.
Psalms 104:19 — He appointed the moon for seasons: the sun knoweth his going down.
Revelation 21:21 — And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; every several gate was of one pearl: and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
